[Athens International Airport]

Athens International Airport Eleftherios Venizelos (IATA: ATH, ICAO: LGAV), commonly initialised as AIA, is the largest international airport in Greece, serving the city of Athens and the region of Attica as well as connecting traffic. It began operation on 28 March 2001 (in time for the 2004 Summer Olympics) and is the main base of Aegean Airlines, as well as other smaller Greek airlines. It replaced the old Ellinikon International Airport.

Athens International Airport is a member of Group 1 of Airports Council International (over 25 million passengers). As of 2025, it is the 15th-busiest airport in Europe and the second busiest and second largest in the Balkans, after Istanbul Airport.

History

Development and ownership

AIA is located between the towns of Markopoulo, Koropi, Spata and Loutsa, about 20 km (12 mi) to the east of central Athens (30 km (19 mi) by road, due to intervening hills). The airport is named after Elefthérios Venizélos. As to-date, the airport is operated by AIA S.A. and ownership is divided between the Hellenic Republic (Greek State) and Private Sector in a 55%-45% stake following a PPP scheme for the airport company. Currently, private investors include the Copelouzos Group (5%) and PSP Investments of Canada (40%), following purchase of Hochtief's shares.

The airport was constructed to replace Athens (Ellinikon) International Airport, which was at capacity with no space for growth. Studies for a new airport had been carried out from as early as the 1970s, with as many as 19 different locations being looked at before an area close to the town of Spata was chosen. [2026 Urda train collision]

On 28 October 2026 at 08:54 CET (UTC+01:00), an AVE high-speed train collided end-on with a stationary Iryo high-speed train in the municipality of Los Yébenes close to the Urda passing and stabling point (PAET), on the Madrid–Seville high-speed rail line, killing 69 people and injuring over 200 more. Both trains were travelling from Atocha station in Madrid to Santa Justa station in Seville.

Government sources gave the likely cause of the crash as human error in the manual operation of signalling, after an automated system had failed.

Background

The high-speed line between Madrid and Seville has two safety systems for the operation of trains, which are known by their initials: LZB and BSL. The LZB automatic signalling system controls train operation by monitoring train speed and location. It ensures that the train is respecting speed limits. LZB can automatically slow down or stop a train if the system detects a dangerous situation. When LZB stops working, the backup system BSL (Bloqueo de Señalización Lateral, or Lateral Signaling Block) is used. With BSL, train drivers must obey track-side signals and observe any speed restrictions. Both systems are automatic, but transition between them when LZB fails is not.

When it fails, LZB can still provide important instructions for train drivers in the form of numeric Meta codes that are displayed in the cab. Two Meta codes are noteworthy. Meta code 40 indicates that the train has lost LZB communication with the central computer, but the track in front of the train is clear and that the train may proceed at a speed no greater than 40 kilometres per hour (25 mph).
